questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: Acid–base balance matters because four listed functions work well only across a narrow pH range. Which set?
opts: Enzyme system, hormonal synthesis, bone turnover and drug metabolism
Oxygenation, oncotic pressure, cardiac conduction and vitamin activation
Enzyme system, muscle and nerve, oxygenation and metabolic function
Clotting cascade, thermoregulation, gut motility and immune surveillance
questions.exp: Acid–base balance matters for the enzyme system, muscle and nerve, oxygenation and metabolic function — all of which function well only across a narrow pH range. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: Per day H⁺ production, as quantified at the start of the chapter, is:
questions.exp: Per day H⁺ production is given as 7 crore nmol (= 70 mmol of fixed acid), while the blood H⁺ concentration at pH 7.4 is 40 nmol/L. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: Blood H⁺ concentration at pH 7.4 is:
questions.exp: Blood H⁺ concentration at pH 7.4 is 40 nmol/L; the daily acid load of 7 crore nmol is far larger, which is why buffering is needed. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: Match the fate of excess H⁺ as printed — 1) Excess H⁺  2) Its cellular effect  3) Final outcome … A) Rendered safe by the buffering system  B) Alters cellular morphology  C) Cellulotoxic
questions.exp: Excess H⁺ → cellulotoxic → alters cellular morphology → rendered safe by buffering system. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: ‘Excess H⁺ is made harmless by altering cellular morphology, without any buffering.’
opts: False — the buffering system renders the H⁺ safe; morphology change is the toxic step
True — morphological change is the neutralising step
True, as long as renal acid excretion is intact
False — H⁺ is removed only by alveolar ventilation
questions.exp: The arrow is the other way round: excess H⁺ is cellulotoxic and alters cellular morphology, and is then rendered safe by the buffering system. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: Match the buffering system to its printed response time — 1) Chemical  2) Respiratory  3) Renal … A) Slow response  B) Immediate response  C) Fast response
questions.exp: Buffering system types: chemical = immediate response, respiratory = fast response, renal = slow response. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: Fill up: The most potent extracellular buffering system is ______.
questions.exp: [H⁺] + [HCO₃⁻] → H₂CO₃ is labelled the most potent extracellular buffering system. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: The general chemical buffering reaction is written as:
questions.exp: Chemical buffering: [H⁺] + [A⁻] (conjugate base) → HA (acid); the particular case with A⁻ = HCO₃⁻ is the most potent extracellular buffer. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: Fill up: pKa is the pH at which ______.
opts: pH equals the PaCO₂ in mmHg
questions.exp: pKa is the pH at which acid state is 50% [A⁻] = 50% [HA]. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: The mechanism of chemical buffering is expressed by which equation?
questions.exp: pH = pKa + log [A⁻] (conjugate base) / [HA] (acid) — the Henderson–Hasselbalch relation as printed under ‘mechanism’. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: ‘A strong acid (pKa < 3) exists more in the HA form and is therefore not good for basic functions.’
opts: True — and weak acids also exist mainly as HA
False — pKa < 3 means the acid exists only as A⁻
True — existing mainly as HA makes strong acids poor buffers
False — strong acids exist mainly as A⁻ and are the best buffers
questions.exp: Strong acid (pKa < 3) exists more in [HA] form: not good for basic functions. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: Which acids are called the best buffer system, and why?
opts: Weak acids — they exist more in the [A⁻] form
Strong acids — they exist more in the [HA] form
Weak acids — they exist more in the [HA] form
Strong acids — they exist more in the [A⁻] form
questions.exp: Weak acids exist more in the [A⁻] form and are therefore the best buffer system, unlike strong acids (pKa < 3) which sit mainly as HA. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering · p819
questions.q: All but one of the following chemical buffers are named in the Book. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: The three chemical buffers printed are the HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃ system, the phosphate buffer and the haemoglobin buffer; an ammonium pair is not listed as a chemical buffer. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: On the Siggaard–Andersen nomogram, the horizontal (x) axis is:
opts: Arterial plasma HCO₃⁻ from 0 to 60 mmol/L
questions.exp: The nomogram's x-axis is arterial blood pH (7.0–7.8); the y-axis is arterial plasma HCO₃⁻ (0–60 mmol/L). (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: On the same nomogram, the vertical (y) axis is:
questions.exp: The y-axis reads arterial plasma HCO₃⁻ in mmol/L, scaled 0–60. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: The right-hand vertical scale of the nomogram (arterial blood [H⁺]) runs:
questions.exp: The right-hand scale is arterial blood [H⁺]: 100 nmol/L at pH 7.0 down to 20 nmol/L at pH 7.8. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: The diagonal lines crossing the nomogram are labelled with pCO₂ from:

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: An ABG shows pH 7.2, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L and pCO₂ 25 mmHg. On the nomogram, this point lies in which labelled zone?
questions.exp: Low pH with a low HCO₃⁻ and a low pCO₂ is the printed ‘Metabolic acidosis’ zone of the nomogram. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: An ABG shows pH 7.52, HCO₃⁻ 44 mmol/L and pCO₂ 55 mmHg. Which nomogram zone is printed for this pattern?
questions.exp: The high-pH/high-HCO₃⁻ corner of the nomogram is labelled ‘Metabolic alkalosis’ (metabolic acidosis sits at low pH with low HCO₃⁻). (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: Match each printed nomogram zone to its pH/bicarbonate pattern — 1) Metabolic acidosis  2) Metabolic alkalosis  3) Chronic respiratory acidosis  4) Acute respiratory alkalosis … A) ↑pH with low HCO₃⁻  B) ↓pH with low HCO₃⁻  C) ↓pH with the greatest HCO₃⁻ rise  D) ↑pH with high HCO₃⁻
questions.exp: Nomogram zones: metabolic acidosis = low pH/low HCO₃⁻; metabolic alkalosis = high pH/high HCO₃⁻; chronic respiratory acidosis = the largest HCO₃⁻ rise for a near-normal pH; acute respiratory alkalosis = high pH with a low HCO₃⁻. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: ‘On the nomogram the “Normal” zone sits at pH 7.4 with HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L and pCO₂ 40 mmHg.’
opts: False — the normal zone sits at pH 7.36 with HCO₃⁻ 40 mEq/L
False — the nomogram has no normal zone marked
True, but only when pCO₂ is 25 mmHg
questions.exp: The central ‘Normal’ box of the Siggaard–Andersen nomogram is the pH 7.4, HCO₃⁻ 24, pCO₂ 40 intersection. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: The arrow diagram beside the chapter title tells us that pH 7.36–7.44 is:
opts: The range of normal PaCO₂ in mmHg
Normal pH — acidosis lies to its left and alkalosis to its right
The range of uncompensated acidosis only
The range at which buffering stops working
questions.exp: Acidosis → Normal pH (7.36–7.44) → Alkalosis, i.e. pH 7.36–7.44 is the normal band with acidosis below and alkalosis above. (Book p819)

questions.sec: Siggaard–Andersen nomogram: axes and regions · p819
questions.q: All but one of these zones are actually printed on the Siggaard–Andersen nomogram. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Printed zones are normal, acute/chronic respiratory acidosis, acute/chronic respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis/alkalosis — there is no mixed high-anion-gap band. (Book p819)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: The HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃ system is described as the first compensation in which disorder?
questions.exp: The HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃ system works as the 1st compensation in metabolic acidosis: [H⁺] + HCO₃⁻. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: Match the fate of carbonic acid in the bicarbonate system — 1) Carbonic acid  2) CO₂ limb  3) H₂O limb … A) Eliminated as water  B) Split into CO₂ and H₂O  C) Exhalation
questions.exp: H₂CO₃ splits into CO₂ (exhalation) and H₂O; the CO₂ limb drives the respiratory compensation. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: After the HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃ buffering step, the fall in PaCO₂ produced by exhalation is called:
questions.exp: ↓PaCO₂ from exhalation is labelled respiratory alkalosis and is the 2nd compensation, following the 1st compensation by HCO₃⁻. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: The pKa of the phosphate buffer is printed as:
questions.exp: Phosphate buffer pKa = 6.8, close to the physiological pH; the haemoglobin buffer pKa is 7.3. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: The phosphate buffer is ranked as:
opts: 2nd most effective, and extracellularly more effective
most effective overall, and equally effective in both compartments
least effective of the three chemical buffers
2nd most effective, and intracellularly more effective
questions.exp: Phosphate buffer: pKa 6.8, 2nd most effective, and more effective intracellularly. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: Fill up: The phosphate buffer reaction is [H⁺] + [HPO₄²⁻] → ______.
questions.exp: Phosphate buffering: [H⁺] + [HPO₄²⁻] → H₂PO₄⁻. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: The pKa of the haemoglobin buffer is:
questions.exp: Haemoglobin buffer: pKa 7.3, most effective intracellular buffering, H⁺ + Hb → HHb. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: Which buffer is called the most effective for intracellular buffering?
questions.exp: Haemoglobin buffer (pKa 7.3) is the most effective intracellular buffering system, reacting H⁺ + Hb → HHb. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: Match each buffer to its pKa and rank — 1) Bicarbonate system  2) Phosphate buffer  3) Haemoglobin buffer … A) pKa 7.3, most effective intracellular buffer  B) pKa 6.8, 2nd most effective buffer  C) Most potent extracellular buffer
questions.exp: Bicarbonate system = most potent extracellular buffer; phosphate = pKa 6.8, 2nd most effective (better intracellularly); haemoglobin = pKa 7.3, most effective intracellular buffer. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: All but one of these statements about the three chemical buffers are printed in the Book. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Haemoglobin buffer reacts H⁺ + Hb → HHb
Bicarbonate buffering in metabolic acidosis is called the 1st compensation
The bicarbonate system is the most effective intracellular buffer
Phosphate buffer has a pKa of 6.8
questions.exp: Intracellular supremacy belongs to haemoglobin (pKa 7.3); the bicarbonate system is the most potent *extracellular* buffer. (Book p820)

questions.sec: The three chemical buffers: bicarbonate, phosphate, haemoglobin · p820
questions.q: ‘Phosphate buffer is more effective inside the cell than outside it.’
opts: False — haemoglobin is the only intracellular buffer
True — but only when pKa rises above 7.4
True — it is described as intracellularly more effective
False — it acts only in plasma
questions.exp: Phosphate buffer (pKa 6.8) is the 2nd most effective and acts intracellularly more effectively. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Match the causes of metabolic acidosis — 1) Acid generation  2) Exogenous acid  3) Endogenous acid  4) Alkali loss … A) GI and renal loss  B) Methanol  C) Ketoacids  D) Parent category
questions.exp: Metabolic acidosis arises from acid generation (exogenous, e.g. methanol; endogenous, e.g. ketoacids) and from alkali loss (GI and renal). (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Fill up: The printed example of an exogenous acid causing metabolic acidosis is ______.
questions.exp: Acid generation is split into exogenous acid (methanol) and endogenous acid (ketoacids). (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Which of the following is given as the endogenous acid example?
questions.exp: Endogenous acid: ketoacids; exogenous acid: methanol. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Match the steps of the anion gap derivation — 1) Total cation vs total anion  2) Adding unmeasured species  3) Measured cation − measured anions … A) = unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation  B) Are equal  C) measured cation + unmeasured cation = measured anion + unmeasured anion
questions.exp: Total cation = total anion; measured cation + unmeasured cation = measured anion + unmeasured anion; hence measured cation − measured anions = unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: The anion gap is defined as which difference, and equals which formula?
opts: Measured anion − measured cation; = (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) − Na⁺
Unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation; = (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)
Unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation; = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)
Unmeasured cation − unmeasured anion; = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)
questions.exp: Anion gap = unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) is also called:
opts: Hypernatremic acidosis, because Na⁺ rises to replace H⁺
Lactic acidosis, because lactate replaces HCO₃⁻
Hyperchloremic acidosis, because HCO₃⁻ is compensated by Cl⁻
questions.exp: In NAGMA, HCO₃⁻ is compensated by Cl⁻, hence the alternative name hyperchloremic acidosis. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Match the NAGMA causes shown in the flowchart — 1) GI loss  2) GI example  3) Renal loss … A) RTA  B) VIPoma  C) Ureterosigmoidostomy
questions.exp: NAGMA causes: GI loss (VIPoma and ureterosigmoidostomy) and renal loss (RTA). (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: A patient with a VIPoma and chronic watery diarrhoea has a normal anion gap acidosis. This fits which printed category?
opts: NAGMA from GI loss of alkali
NAGMA from renal loss of alkali
questions.exp: VIPoma is printed under NAGMA – GI loss, whereas RTA is the renal loss cause. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: High anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) is characterised by:
questions.exp: HAGMA: ↑ in unmeasured anions — the unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation difference widens. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Fill up: The mnemonic given for the causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis is ______.
questions.exp: HAGMA causes are remembered by KUSMAL — ketoacidosis, uremia, salicylates/paraldehyde, methanol, ethylene glycol (alcohol) and lactic acidosis. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Match the KUSMAL letters to their causes — 1) K  2) U  3) S  4) L … A) Lactic acidosis  B) Ketoacidosis  C) Salicylates/Paraldehyde  D) Uremia
questions.exp: KUSMAL: K = ketoacidosis, U = uremia, S = salicylates/paraldehyde, M = methanol, A = ethylene glycol (alcohol), L = lactic acidosis. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: Under ‘K’ of the KUSMAL mnemonic, the three printed ketoacidosis subtypes are:
questions.exp: Ketoacidosis (i) DKA (ii) starvation (iii) alcoholic. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: A patient swallows antifreeze and develops a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap and an osmolal gap. Which KUSMAL entry explains it?
questions.exp: Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) is printed as ‘Ethylene glycol (Alcohol)’ under KUSMAL and produces HAGMA. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA · p820
questions.q: All but one of the following belong to the KUSMAL list of HAGMA causes. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: KUSMAL lists ketoacidosis, uremia, salicylates/paraldehyde, methanol, ethylene glycol and lactic acidosis — paracetamol is not part of it. (Book p820)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: Acidemia is defined as blood pH:
questions.exp: Acidemia: blood pH < 7.36; alkalemia: blood pH > 7.44. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: Alkalemia is defined as blood pH:
questions.exp: Alkalemia: blood pH > 7.44 (acidemia is < 7.36). (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: Match the terminology box — 1) Acidemia  2) Acidosis  3) Alkalemia  4) Alkalosis … A) If alkalemia left unopposed  B) Blood pH < 7.36  C) If acidemia left unopposed  D) Blood pH > 7.44
questions.exp: Acidemia = pH < 7.36; acidosis = if acidemia left unopposed. Alkalemia = pH > 7.44; alkalosis = if alkalemia left unopposed. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: ‘Acidemia and acidosis mean exactly the same thing, and so do alkalemia and alkalosis.’
opts: False — acidosis refers only to a raised PaCO₂
True, but only for respiratory disorders
False — acidemia/alkalemia are the pH findings; acidosis/alkalosis are those states left unopposed
True — the terms are used interchangeably in the chapter
questions.exp: The distinction is printed: acidemia = pH < 7.36 and acidosis = if acidemia is left unopposed; likewise for alkalemia/alkalosis. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: At pH 7.4 the H⁺ concentration is 40 nmol/L. Using the printed multipliers, H⁺ at pH 7.3 is:
questions.exp: Moving 0.1 pH below 7.4 multiplies H⁺ by 1.25: 40 × 1.25 = 50 nmol/L. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: Using the same multipliers, H⁺ at pH 7.2 is:
questions.exp: Two 0.1-pH steps below 7.4: 40 × 1.25 × 1.25 = 63 nmol/L (the printed value at pH 7.2). (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: Moving 0.1 pH above 7.4, the printed multiplier is ×0.8 — so H⁺ at pH 7.5 is:
questions.exp: × 0.8 per 0.1 pH rise: 40 × 0.8 = 32 nmol/L at pH 7.5. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: H⁺ concentration printed at pH 7.6 is:
questions.exp: The printed ladder is pH 7.2 = 63, 7.3 = 50, 7.4 = 40, 7.5 = 32 and 7.6 = 25 nmol/L. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: Match the pH and H⁺ pairs printed in the H⁺ ion estimation diagram — 1) pH 7.2  2) pH 7.3  3) pH 7.5  4) pH 7.6 … A) 25 nmol/L  B) 63 nmol/L  C) 32 nmol/L  D) 50 nmol/L
questions.exp: Printed pairs: pH 7.2 → 63, pH 7.3 → 50, pH 7.4 → 40, pH 7.5 → 32, pH 7.6 → 25 nmol/L. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Basic terminology and H⁺ estimation from pH · p821
questions.q: A resident estimates H⁺ as 40 nmol/L and notes the patient's pH is 7.3. Would you correct the resident?
opts: No — the estimate is valid because pH and H⁺ are unrelated
Yes — at pH 7.3 H⁺ should be 50 nmol/L (×1.25 per 0.1 pH fall)
No — 40 nmol/L holds for any pH between 7.2 and 7.6
Yes — at pH 7.3 H⁺ should be 63 nmol/L
questions.exp: 40 nmol/L is the value at pH 7.4; each 0.1 pH fall multiplies H⁺ by 1.25, giving 50 nmol/L at pH 7.3. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: Match the respiratory buffering chain — 1) [H⁺] + HCO₃⁻  2) CO₂ drive out  3) Consequence … A) ↑ respiratory rate produces respiratory alkalosis  B) Forms H₂CO₃  C) ↓ PaCO₂
questions.exp: Respiratory buffering: [H⁺] + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃; CO₂ is driven out by ↑ respiratory rate (respiratory alkalosis), lowering PaCO₂. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: Which statement about the respiratory buffering system is printed?
opts: CO₂ excretion is independent of respiratory rate
CO₂ is driven out by an increased respiratory rate, causing respiratory alkalosis and ↓ PaCO₂
CO₂ is retained by a fall in respiratory rate, causing respiratory acidosis and ↑ PaCO₂
CO₂ is converted to HCO₃⁻ in the alveolus
questions.exp: In respiratory buffering, CO₂ drive out occurs with ↑ respiratory rate → respiratory alkalosis → ↓PaCO₂. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: Match the acids produced by the kidney — 1) Non-volatile acids  2) Examples of non-volatile acids  3) Volatile acid  4) Elimination of the volatile acid … A) By respiration  B) Sulphuric acid and phosphoric acid  C) H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid) → H₂O + CO₂  D) Parent category
questions.exp: Kidney-produced acids: non-volatile acids (sulphuric acid, phosphoric acid) and the volatile H₂CO₃ which breaks to H₂O + CO₂ and is eliminated by respiration. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: Renal excretion of non-volatile acid is stated as:
questions.exp: Excretion is 1 mEq/kg/day, i.e. about 80 mEq/day, excreted as titratable acid and ammonia. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: The 80 mEq of daily acid load is excreted in which two forms?
questions.exp: Excretion 1 mEq/kg/day (80 mEq/day) as titratable acid and ammonia. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: Filtered HCO₃⁻ per day is printed as 4330 mEq. How is that figure derived?
questions.exp: HCO₃⁻ glomerular filtration = 4330 mEq, i.e. 24 mEq/L × 180 L/day. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: Fill up: Urine excretion of HCO₃⁻ is ______.
questions.exp: Urine excretion of HCO₃⁻ is nil because reabsorption is 100% (4000 of the 4330 mEq in the PCT alone). (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: The reabsorption of filtered HCO₃⁻ is 100%, distributed in which printed order of magnitude?
questions.exp: Reabsorption is 100%: PCT (approx 4000 mEq) > thick AL > DCT; the rest of the filtered load is reclaimed more distally. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: ‘About 4000 of the 4330 mEq of filtered bicarbonate is reabsorbed in the PCT, and the urine ultimately contains none.’
opts: False — urine normally contains 80 mEq/day of HCO₃⁻
True, but the distal nephron contributes the larger share
True — PCT ≈ 4000 mEq, overall reabsorption 100%, urine HCO₃⁻ nil
False — the PCT reabsorbs only about 400 mEq
questions.exp: Filtered HCO₃⁻ 4330 mEq/day is 100% reabsorbed — approximately 4000 mEq in the PCT, the rest in thick AL and DCT — so urine HCO₃⁻ excretion is nil. (Book p821)

questions.sec: Respiratory and renal buffering systems · p821
questions.q: All but one of these are printed under the renal buffering system. Which is the odd one out?
opts: 80 mEq of volatile acid excreted daily
questions.exp: The 80 mEq/day refers to *non-volatile* acid excretion; volatile H₂CO₃ is eliminated by respiration, not excreted in urine. (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: In the PCT diagram, which transporter sits on the luminal membrane of the proximal tubule cell?
questions.exp: The luminal membrane carries the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger; the basolateral membrane carries the Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger. (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: Step ① of the PCT diagram — the hydration/dehydration of carbonic acid in the lumen — is catalysed by:
opts: No enzyme — the step is spontaneous
questions.exp: Step ① is luminal carbonic anhydrase IV acting on HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂CO₃; step ③ is cytoplasmic CA II. (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: Step ③ inside the PCT cell, generating H₂CO₃ from CO₂ and H₂O, is catalysed by:
questions.exp: Cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase II (CA II) hydrates CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ inside the cell; the luminal enzyme is CA IV. (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: Match the numbered PCT steps — 1) Step ①  2) Step ②  3) Step ③  4) Step ④ … A) Dissociation of H₂CO₃ into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻  B) CA IV acting on HCO₃⁻ and H⁺  C) CA II forming H₂CO₃ from CO₂ and H₂O  D) Splitting of H₂CO₃ into H₂O and CO₂
questions.exp: Luminal CA IV forms H₂CO₃ (①), which splits to H₂O + CO₂ (②); CO₂ enters the cell and CA II rebuilds H₂CO₃ (③), which dissociates to H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ (④). (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: How does the HCO₃⁻ formed inside the PCT cell leave for the blood side?
opts: By simple diffusion across the luminal membrane
questions.exp: The regenerated HCO₃⁻ exits across the basolateral membrane on the Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger, while H⁺ leaves apically on the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger. (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: Match the arrows entering the PCT cell from the lumen — 1) H₂O  2) Na⁺  3) Ca²⁺ … A) Reabsorbed cation named third  B) Reabsorbed cation named second  C) Reabsorbed with the filtrate solvent
questions.exp: The diagram shows H₂O, Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ reabsorbed from lumen into the PCT cell along with CO₂. (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: Fill up: In the PCT diagram, CA stands for ______.
questions.exp: CA = carbonic anhydrase, the enzyme family catalysing the luminal (CA IV) and cytoplasmic (CA II) steps. (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the PCT. Predict the effect from the printed diagram.
opts: Both the luminal CA IV and cytoplasmic CA II steps fail, so HCO₃⁻ reabsorption falls
Only the basolateral Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger is inhibited
HCO₃⁻ reabsorption increases because H₂CO₃ accumulates
Only the Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger is inhibited, sparing HCO₃⁻
questions.exp: The diagram places CA IV luminally (step ①) and CA II in the cytoplasm (step ③); blocking carbonic anhydrase breaks both steps of HCO₃⁻ reabsorption. (Book p821)

questions.sec: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram · p821
questions.q: All but one of these are shown moving across the luminal border of the PCT cell in the diagram. Which is the odd one out?
opts: HCO₃⁻ moving from blood into the lumen
questions.exp: The diagram shows Na⁺, CO₂ and H₂O entering the cell and H⁺ leaving into the lumen; HCO₃⁻ movement is basolateral, into the blood. (Book p821)

questions.sec: The 4400 mEq H⁺ requirement and buffering · p822
questions.q: For reabsorption of 1 mEq of HCO₃⁻, how much H⁺ is used?
opts: No H⁺ — it is a passive step
questions.exp: For 1 mEq HCO₃⁻ reabsorption, 1 mEq of H⁺ is used — the basis of the daily H⁺ requirement. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The 4400 mEq H⁺ requirement and buffering · p822
questions.q: Adding the 4330 mEq of filtered HCO₃⁻ to the 80 mEq of non-volatile acid gives a daily requirement of:
questions.exp: 4330 mEq of HCO₃⁻ + 80 mEq of non-volatile acid = 4400 mEq of H⁺ required, which the book calls not practically possible. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The 4400 mEq H⁺ requirement and buffering · p822
questions.q: Because 4400 mEq of H⁺ per day is not practically possible, the book concludes:
opts: The kidney must excrete 4400 mEq of titratable acid
Bicarbonate filtration must fall to 4000 mEq/day
Respiratory compensation alone must handle the load
There is a requirement of the buffering system
questions.exp: 4400 mEq of H⁺ required (not practically possible) → requirement of buffering system. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The 4400 mEq H⁺ requirement and buffering · p822
questions.q: Match the quantities used to reach the daily H⁺ requirement — 1) Filtered HCO₃⁻  2) Non-volatile acid  3) Total H⁺ required … A) 80 mEq  B) 4400 mEq  C) 4330 mEq
questions.exp: 4330 mEq of HCO₃⁻ plus 80 mEq of non-volatile acid demands 4400 mEq of H⁺ per day. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The 4400 mEq H⁺ requirement and buffering · p822
questions.q: ‘The kidney alone can secrete the 4400 mEq of H⁺ needed each day, without any buffering.’
opts: True — because urine HCO₃⁻ excretion is nil
False — because only 80 mEq of H⁺ is needed daily
False — the book calls 4400 mEq of H⁺ not practically possible and invokes buffering
True — tubular secretion covers it entirely
questions.exp: 4400 mEq of H⁺ per day is explicitly labelled ‘not practically possible’, which is why the buffering system is required. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The 4400 mEq H⁺ requirement and buffering · p822
questions.q: A student computes daily H⁺ need as 4330 mEq from filtered bicarbonate alone. What has been left out?
opts: The 7 crore nmol excreted as ammonia
The 80 mEq of non-volatile acid, giving 4400 mEq
The 4000 mEq reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb
questions.exp: The 4330 mEq of filtered HCO₃⁻ must be added to the 80 mEq of non-volatile acid, giving the printed total of 4400 mEq of H⁺. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: Renal tubular acidosis type 2 is defined as:
opts: Isolated failure of the distal H⁺-ATPase
questions.exp: RTA type 2 = generalised dysfunction of the PCT (proximal RTA). (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: Match the type 2 RTA defect — 1) Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger defect  2) Carbonic anhydrase defect  3) Overall description … A) Generalised dysfunction of the PCT  B) Enzyme defect  C) Exchanger defect
questions.exp: The defect in type 2 RTA is a Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger defect and/or a carbonic anhydrase defect. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: In childhood, type 2 RTA is caused by Fanconi's syndrome. Which is the most common underlying cause?
questions.exp: Childhood causes: Fanconi's syndrome — cystinosis (m/c), Lowe's disease, and Wilson disease in adolescence. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: Match the childhood causes of type 2 RTA to their age label — 1) Cystinosis  2) Lowe's disease  3) Wilson disease … A) Labelled adolescence  B) Most common cause  C) Also listed under Fanconi's syndrome
questions.exp: Cystinosis is the m/c childhood cause, Lowe's disease is listed alongside it, and Wilson disease is tagged as adolescence. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: A 16-year-old with tremor, Kayser–Fleischer rings and a proximal renal tubular acidosis — which printed cause fits best?
questions.exp: Wilson disease appears under the childhood/Fanconi causes of type 2 RTA and is specifically tagged ‘adolescence’. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: Match the adults' causes of type 2 RTA — 1) Haematological cause  2) Antiviral drug  3) Antibiotic … A) Gentamicin  B) Myeloma  C) Tenofovir
questions.exp: Adult causes: myeloma and drugs — tenofovir, cyclophosphamide, outdated tetracycline and gentamicin. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: Which quartet of drugs is printed as a cause of adult type 2 RTA?
questions.exp: Drugs causing type 2 RTA in adults: tenofovir, cyclophosphamide, outdated tetracycline and gentamicin. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: ‘Type 2 RTA is an isolated defect of bicarbonate reabsorption with everything else in the PCT working normally.’
opts: False — type 2 RTA spares the PCT and affects the distal tubule only
False — it is a generalised dysfunction of the PCT, so phosphate and glucose handling also fail
True — only the Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger is ever affected
True — that is why there is no glycosuria
questions.exp: Type 2 RTA is a *generalised* PCT dysfunction: bicarbonate, phosphate and glucose handling all fail, hence rickets-like changes and glycosuria. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Proximal (type 2) RTA: defect and causes · p822
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed causes of type 2 RTA. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Sjögren's syndrome is the acquired cause of *distal* RTA; type 2 RTA's causes are Fanconi's syndrome (cystinosis m/c, Lowe's, Wilson) and myeloma/drugs (tenofovir, cyclophosphamide, outdated tetracycline, gentamicin). (Book p822)

questions.sec: Consequences of the PCT defect in type 2 RTA · p822
questions.q: Match the three arms of the PCT-defect flowchart — 1) HCO₃⁻ not reabsorbed  2) Na⁺–phosphorus exchange defect  3) Na⁺–glucose transporter inactive … A) Glycosuria  B) NAGMA  C) Loss of phosphorus
questions.exp: Three arms: HCO₃⁻ not reabsorbed → NAGMA; Na⁺–phosphorus exchange defect → loss of phosphorus → rickets-like changes; Na⁺–glucose transporter inactive → glycosuria. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Consequences of the PCT defect in type 2 RTA · p822
questions.q: Match the cascade that follows failed HCO₃⁻ reabsorption — 1) First step  2) Next  3) Then  4) End … A) Hypokalemia  B) NAGMA  C) RAS activation  D) RTA-II: salt water wasting
questions.exp: HCO₃⁻ not reabsorbed → NAGMA → RTA-II with salt water wasting → defective arteriolar volume → RAS activation → hypokalemia. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Consequences of the PCT defect in type 2 RTA · p822
questions.q: Loss of phosphorus in type 2 RTA produces:
questions.exp: Na⁺–phosphorus exchange defect → loss of phosphorus → rickets-like changes. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Consequences of the PCT defect in type 2 RTA · p822
questions.q: Glycosuria in type 2 RTA results from:
opts: Loss of phosphorus from the PCT
questions.exp: Na⁺–glucose transporter inactive → glycosuria (in the presence of a generalised PCT defect). (Book p822)

questions.sec: Consequences of the PCT defect in type 2 RTA · p822
questions.q: A child with proximal RTA has polyuria, salt craving, low blood pressure and hypokalemia on the ABG. What sequence explains it?
opts: Salt water wasting → defective arteriolar volume → RAS activation → hypokalemia
questions.exp: The printed cascade for RTA-II is salt water wasting → defective arteriolar volume → RAS activation → hypokalemia. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Consequences of the PCT defect in type 2 RTA · p822
questions.q: ‘Salt wasting in type 2 RTA leads to RAS activation, and the resulting aldosterone effect is hypokalemia.’
opts: True, but the hypokalemia comes from the phosphate leak
False — salt wasting is seen only in distal RTA
True — defective arteriolar volume drives RAS activation and hence hypokalemia
questions.exp: Defective arteriolar volume activates the RAS, and the endpoint printed in the flowchart is hypokalemia. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Consequences of the PCT defect in type 2 RTA · p822
questions.q: All but one of these are consequences of the generalised PCT defect. Which is the odd one out?
opts: NAGMA with salt and water wasting
Loss of phosphorus with rickets-like changes
questions.exp: An alkaline urine pH belongs to distal RTA; in proximal RTA the urine pH is normal, and the printed consequences are NAGMA, phosphaturia and glycosuria. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: The cortical collecting system diagram is drawn for which cell type?
questions.exp: The diagram is labelled ‘α intercalated cell’, the acid-secreting cell of the cortical collecting system. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: Match the pumps on the α-intercalated cell — 1) Luminal H⁺ pump  2) Apical exchange pump  3) Which ion is exchanged … A) K⁺  B) H⁺-ATPase  C) H⁺,K⁺-ATPase
questions.exp: Both an H⁺-ATPase and an H⁺,K⁺-ATPase are drawn on the luminal side of the α-intercalated cell, the latter exchanging H⁺ for K⁺. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: How many ATP-requiring pumps are labelled in the α-intercalated cell diagram?
questions.exp: The diagram labels two ATP-dependent transporters: the H⁺-ATPase and the H⁺,K⁺-ATPase. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: Fill up: Inside the α-intercalated cell, CO₂ + H₂O combine under the influence of ______ to form H₂CO₃.
questions.exp: The α-intercalated cell uses CA II to make H₂CO₃ from CO₂ and H₂O; the H⁺ so generated is secreted into the lumen. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: Match the urinary acid species — 1) HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻  2) NH₃ → NH₄⁺  3) Difference between them … A) Non-titratable acid  B) Titratable acid  C) Only the first appears on the titratable-acid line
questions.exp: The diagram labels HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻ as titratable acid and NH₃ → NH₄⁺ as non-titratable acid. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: Fill up: Net acid secretion = urine NH₄⁺ + ______ − urine HCO₃⁻.
questions.exp: Net acid secretion: urine NH₄⁺ + urine titratable acid − urine HCO₃⁻. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: In the α-intercalated cell diagram, the K⁺ drawn on the luminal side moves:
opts: Into the lumen, exchanged for H⁺ by the H⁺,K⁺-ATPase
Into the cell, exchanged for Na⁺
Into the lumen, pumped by the H⁺-ATPase
Nowhere — K⁺ is shown only intracellularly
questions.exp: The H⁺,K⁺-ATPase exchanges H⁺ (secreted) for K⁺ (reabsorbed); K⁺ is also shown exiting to the lumen alongside H⁺ in the diagram. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: ‘The urinary ammonium and phosphate species are both counted as titratable acid in the printed formula.’
opts: False — NH₄⁺ is non-titratable acid; only the phosphate species is titratable acid
True — both are titratable acid by definition
False — HPO₄²⁻ is the non-titratable species
True, but only when urine HCO₃⁻ is zero
questions.exp: The diagram labels H₂PO₄⁻ (from HPO₄²⁻) as titratable acid and NH₄⁺ as non-titratable acid; the net acid formula adds both to urine NH₄⁺ and subtracts urine HCO₃⁻. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: All but one of these are labelled on the α-intercalated cell diagram. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: The luminal membrane shows the H⁺-ATPase and the H⁺,K⁺-ATPase with CA II in the cytoplasm; no luminal Na⁺–K⁺-ATPase is drawn. (Book p822)

questions.sec: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion · p822
questions.q: A patient's urine shows abundant NH₄⁺ and H₂PO₄⁻ but no HCO₃⁻. What is the net acid secretion according to the printed formula?
opts: Zero, because urine HCO₃⁻ is nil
Urine NH₄⁺ + urine titratable acid (urine HCO₃⁻ contributes nothing)
questions.exp: Net acid secretion = urine NH₄⁺ + urine titratable acid − urine HCO₃⁻; with no urinary HCO₃⁻, the two acid species alone determine net acid secretion. (Book p822)

questions.sec: Distal (type 1) RTA · p823
questions.q: Distal RTA (type 1) is caused by a defect of:
questions.exp: Distal RTA/type 1: defect of the H⁺-ATPase / H⁺,K⁺-ATPase of the distal tubule. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal (type 1) RTA · p823
questions.q: Match the consequences of the distal tubular defect — 1) Acid–base defect  2) Potassium  3) Urine pH … A) Alkaline  B) Severe NAGMA  C) Severe hypokalemia
questions.exp: Distal tubular defect → severe NAGMA, severe hypokalemia and an alkaline urine pH, with no glycosuria. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal (type 1) RTA · p823
questions.q: ‘Glycosuria is a feature of distal RTA.’
opts: True, but only in the acquired form
False — glycosuria occurs in distal RTA only with diabetes
False — the flowchart states ‘No glycosuria’ in distal RTA
True — the distal tubule normally reclaims glucose
questions.exp: The distal RTA flowchart explicitly prints ‘No glycosuria’ (glycosuria belongs to proximal RTA). (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal (type 1) RTA · p823
questions.q: Match the bone/stone arm of distal RTA — 1) Ca²⁺ resorption in bone  2) Result one  3) Result two … A) Kidney stones  B) ↑Ca²⁺ resorption in bone  C) Rickets-like change
questions.exp: Increased Ca²⁺ resorption from bone in distal RTA produces rickets-like change and kidney stones. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal (type 1) RTA · p823
questions.q: A 34-year-old woman has severe hypokalemia, a hyperchloremic acidosis with a normal anion gap, an alkaline urine and recurrent calcium stones. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.exp: Severe NAGMA with severe hypokalemia, alkaline urine, rickets-like change and kidney stones is the printed picture of distal RTA/type 1. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal (type 1) RTA · p823
questions.q: Salt and water wasting in distal RTA leads to:
questions.exp: The distal RTA flowchart: salt water wasting → RANS activation (the printed spelling alongside RAS). (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal (type 1) RTA · p823
questions.q: All but one of these are features of distal RTA on the flowchart. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: Distal RTA produces severe NAGMA, severe hypokalemia, salt wasting and an alkaline urine — the chart states ‘No glycosuria’. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal (type 1) RTA · p823
questions.q: ‘In distal RTA the acidosis and the hypokalemia are both described as severe, while in proximal RTA they are mild.’
opts: False — both are severe in proximal RTA
True — but only the hypokalemia is severe in distal RTA
False — the table says NAGMA is mild in distal RTA
True — the comparison table grades them severe in distal and mild in proximal RTA
questions.exp: The distal-vs-proximal table grades NAGMA with hypokalemia as severe in distal RTA and mild in proximal RTA. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: Match the two RTA columns to the table rows — 1) Kidney stones  2) Urine pH  3) Glycosuria … A) Absent (proximal RTA)  B) Present (distal RTA)  C) Alkaline (distal RTA)
questions.exp: Distal RTA: kidney stones present, urine pH alkaline, glycosuria absent. Proximal RTA reverses all three. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: In proximal RTA the urine pH is best described as:
opts: Fixed at 5.0 whatever the systemic pH
Normal, because the distal acidification machinery is intact
questions.exp: Proximal RTA has a normal urine pH whereas distal RTA has an alkaline urine pH. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: Rickets in distal RTA is due to ______, while in proximal RTA it is due to ______.
opts: loss of phosphorus; loss of phosphorus
questions.exp: Table row ‘Rickets’: distal RTA — due to (D/t) Ca²⁺ resorption; proximal RTA — due to loss of phosphorus. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: A patient with RTA has rickets and NO kidney stones but does pass glucose in urine with normal blood sugar. Which column of the table is this?
opts: Proximal RTA — glycosuria absent, stones present
Distal RTA — glycosuria absent, stones absent
Proximal RTA — glycosuria present, stones absent
Distal RTA — glycosuria present, stones absent
questions.exp: Glycosuria with absent kidney stones identifies the proximal RTA column of the table. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: Match the inherited causes row — 1) Distal RTA  2) Proximal RTA  3) Mode of distal inheritance … A) Fanconi's syndrome  B) Autosomal recessive  C) H⁺ ATPase / H⁺ K⁺ ATPase defect
questions.exp: Inherited row: distal RTA — autosomal recessive H⁺ ATPase / H⁺ K⁺ ATPase defect; proximal RTA — Fanconi's syndrome. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: The acquired cause listed for distal RTA is ______ and for proximal RTA is ______.
questions.exp: Acquired row of the table: distal RTA — Sjögren's syndrome; proximal RTA — myeloma. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: Match each item to the RTA type it belongs to — 1) Sjögren's syndrome  2) Myeloma  3) Fanconi's syndrome  4) Autosomal recessive H⁺ ATPase defect … A) Proximal RTA acquired  B) Distal RTA inherited  C) Distal RTA acquired  D) Proximal RTA inherited
questions.exp: Sjögren's = distal acquired; myeloma = proximal acquired; Fanconi's syndrome = proximal inherited; AR H⁺ ATPase/H⁺ K⁺ ATPase defect = distal inherited. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: ‘Kidney stones are present in distal RTA but absent in proximal RTA, while glycosuria behaves the opposite way.’
opts: False — stones are present in both types
False — glycosuria is present in both types
True, except that stones are also present in proximal RTA
True — stones present/absent and glycosuria absent/present respectively
questions.exp: The table prints stones Present (distal) / Absent (proximal) and glycosuria Absent (distal) / Present (proximal). (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: Two patients both have NAGMA. One has severe hypokalemia with an alkaline urine; the other has mild hypokalemia with a normal urine pH. Which is which?
opts: Both are proximal RTA; urine pH is unrelated
First is distal RTA, second is proximal RTA
First is proximal RTA, second is distal RTA
Both are distal RTA, differing only in severity
questions.exp: Severe NAGMA with hypokalemia and an alkaline urine = distal RTA; mild NAGMA with hypokalemia and a normal urine pH = proximal RTA. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: All but one of these are correctly paired in the distal vs proximal RTA table. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Kidney stones — absent in distal RTA
Urine pH — alkaline in distal RTA
NAGMA with hypokalemia — severe in distal RTA
questions.exp: Kidney stones are *present* in distal RTA and absent in proximal RTA; the other three pairings are as printed. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Distal vs proximal RTA table, row by row · p823
questions.q: Which single table row best separates distal from proximal RTA at the bedside?
opts: Serum bicarbonate — always normal in proximal RTA
Anion gap — raised in distal RTA only
Urine pH — alkaline in distal RTA versus normal in proximal RTA
Serum potassium — always normal in distal RTA
questions.exp: Both types show NAGMA, so the discriminating rows are urine pH (alkaline vs normal), stones (present vs absent) and glycosuria (absent vs present). (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: Fill up: Urine anion gap = urinary Na⁺ + urinary K⁺ − ______.
questions.exp: UAG = urinary Na⁺ + urinary K⁺ − urinary Cl⁻ = unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: The urine anion gap is best described as:
opts: Strongly positive, being unmeasured cation − unmeasured anion
Always zero because urine is electroneutral
Equal to the serum anion gap
Slightly negative, being unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation
questions.exp: The urine anion gap (urinary Na⁺ + K⁺ − Cl⁻ = unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation) is slightly negative normally. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: Match the urine anion gap result to its significance — 1) Positive UAG  2) Negative UAG  3) Normal UAG … A) Slightly negative  B) GI loss  C) RTA
questions.exp: UAG significance: positive → RTA; negative → GI loss. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: A patient with a normal anion gap acidosis has a negative urine anion gap. Where is the bicarbonate being lost?
questions.exp: A negative urine anion gap points to GI loss; a positive gap points to renal tubular acidosis. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: ‘Ammonia formation occurs predominantly in the proximal tubules.’
opts: False — ammonia is made mainly in the distal tubule
False — ammonia is made mainly in the collecting duct
True, but only during metabolic alkalosis
True — the note states formation of ammonia is predominantly in the proximal tubules
questions.exp: Note: formation of ammonia is predominantly in the proximal tubules; the reaction chain is glutamine → glutamate → α-keto glutarate. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: Match the ammonia-forming pathway — 1) Starting amino acid  2) First product  3) Second product … A) Glutamine  B) α-keto glutarate  C) Glutamate
questions.exp: Glutamine → glutamate → α-keto glutarate, with NH₃ released at each step. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: How many NH₃ molecules are shown being released along the printed pathway?
opts: None — NH₃ is released only in the distal tubule
Two — one from glutamine and one from glutamate
questions.exp: The pathway glutamine → glutamate → α-keto glutarate shows an NH₃ released at each of the two steps. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: A patient with diarrhoea has a normal anion gap acidosis. Which urine anion gap and ammonia pattern do you expect?
opts: Positive UAG with a blunted ammonia response
Negative UAG with a blunted ammonia response
Positive UAG with a brisk proximal ammonia response
Negative UAG with a brisk proximal ammonia response
questions.exp: GI loss gives a negative urine anion gap and, unlike RTA, the proximal tubules respond by making more ammonia from glutamine. (Book p823)

questions.sec: Urine anion gap and ammonia formation · p823
questions.q: All but one of these are printed in the urine anion gap section. Which is the odd one out?
opts: A positive UAG indicates gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate
UAG = urinary Na⁺ + urinary K⁺ − urinary Cl⁻
Ammonia formation occurs predominantly in the proximal tubules
questions.exp: A positive UAG indicates RTA; it is the *negative* UAG that indicates GI loss. (Book p823)

units.title: Acid–base balance, H⁺ load and chemical buffering
units.guide: Functions work only across a narrow pH range; daily H⁺ production is 7 crore nmol against a blood H⁺ of 40 nmol/L at pH 7.4. Excess H⁺ is cellulotoxic, altering cellular morphology before the buffering system renders it safe. Buffering types: chemical (immediate), respiratory (fast), renal (slow). Chemical buffering = [H⁺] + [A⁻] → HA, with H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ the most potent extracellular buffer; pKa is the pH at which 50% A⁻ = 50% HA, and weak acids (mostly A⁻) are the best buffers.

units.title: The Siggaard–Andersen nomogram and the three buffer types
units.guide: Nomogram: x-axis arterial pH 7.0–7.8, y-axis arterial plasma HCO₃⁻ 0–60 mmol/L, right-hand [H⁺] scale 100→20 nmol/L, isobars labelled pCO₂ 120→10 mmHg, and printed zones for normal, acute/chronic respiratory acidosis and alkalosis, and metabolic acidosis/alkalosis. Buffer types: bicarbonate system (1st compensation in metabolic acidosis, CO₂ exhaled so PaCO₂ falls = 2nd compensation), phosphate (pKa 6.8, 2nd most effective, better intracellularly) and haemoglobin (pKa 7.3, best intracellular buffer).

units.title: Metabolic acidosis, the anion gap and NAGMA/HAGMA
units.guide: Causes of metabolic acidosis = acid generation (exogenous: methanol; endogenous: ketoacids) and alkali loss (GI and renal). Anion gap derivation from measured/unmeasured cations and anions, giving AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). NAGMA = hyperchloremic acidosis with GI loss (VIPoma, ureterosigmoidostomy) and renal loss (RTA); HAGMA = rise in unmeasured anions with the KUSMAL list — ketoacidosis (DKA, starvation, alcoholic), uremia, salicylates/paraldehyde, methanol, ethylene glycol (alcohol) and lactic acidosis.

units.title: Terminology, H⁺ estimation and the buffering systems
units.guide: Acidemia < 7.36, alkalemia > 7.44, with acidosis/alkalosis defined as those states left unopposed. H⁺ estimation: 40 nmol/L at pH 7.4, ×1.25 per 0.1 pH fall, ×0.8 per 0.1 pH rise (7.2 = 63, 7.3 = 50, 7.5 = 32, 7.6 = 25). Respiratory buffering drives CO₂ out with ↑ respiratory rate → respiratory alkalosis → ↓PaCO₂. Renal buffering: non-volatile acids (sulphuric, phosphoric) excreted 1 mEq/kg/day (80 mEq/day) as titratable acid and ammonia; volatile H₂CO₃ is exhaled. 4330 mEq/day of HCO₃⁻ (24 × 180 L) is filtered and 100% reabsorbed — PCT ≈ 4000 mEq > thick AL > DCT — so urine HCO₃⁻ is nil.

units.title: PCT bicarbonate reabsorption: the CA IV / CA II diagram
units.guide: Luminal Na⁺–H⁺ exchanger; luminal CA IV converts HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ to H₂CO₃ (step ①), which splits into H₂O + CO₂ (step ②). CO₂ enters the cell where CA II rebuilds H₂CO₃ (step ③), which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻ (step ④); HCO₃⁻ leaves on the basolateral Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger. H₂O, Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ are reabsorbed along with CO₂.

units.title: Proximal (type 2) RTA: the 4400 mEq H⁺ problem and the PCT defect
units.guide: For 1 mEq HCO₃⁻ reabsorbed, 1 mEq H⁺ is used; 4330 mEq of HCO₃⁻ plus 80 mEq of non-volatile acid demands 4400 mEq H⁺ daily — not practically possible, hence the requirement of the buffering system. Type 2 RTA = generalised PCT dysfunction from a Na⁺–HCO₃⁻ exchanger or carbonic anhydrase defect: Fanconi's syndrome in childhood (cystinosis m/c, Lowe's disease, Wilson disease in adolescence) and myeloma or drugs (tenofovir, cyclophosphamide, outdated tetracycline, gentamicin) in adults. The PCT defect cascades to NAGMA, salt water wasting, RAS activation and hypokalemia; the phosphate arm gives rickets-like changes and the glucose arm glycosuria.

units.title: The α-intercalated cell and net acid secretion
units.guide: Cortical collecting system diagram of the α-intercalated cell: luminal H⁺-ATPase and H⁺,K⁺-ATPase (both ATP-dependent), cytoplasmic CA II making H₂CO₃ from CO₂ and H₂O, and H⁺ secreted into the lumen. HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻ is titratable acid and NH₃ → NH₄⁺ is non-titratable acid. Net acid secretion = urine NH₄⁺ + urine titratable acid − urine HCO₃⁻.

units.title: Distal (type 1) RTA and the distal vs proximal RTA table
units.guide: Distal RTA = H⁺-ATPase / H⁺,K⁺-ATPase defect, giving severe NAGMA, severe hypokalemia, salt water wasting with RANS activation, ↑Ca²⁺ resorption in bone with rickets-like change and kidney stones, an alkaline urine and no glycosuria. The distal vs proximal table: severity of NAGMA + hypokalemia (severe vs mild), mechanism of rickets (Ca²⁺ resorption vs loss of phosphorus), stones (present vs absent), urine pH (alkaline vs normal), glycosuria (absent vs present), inherited causes (AR H⁺ ATPase/H⁺ K⁺ ATPase defect vs Fanconi's syndrome) and acquired causes (Sjögren's syndrome vs myeloma).

units.title: Urine anion gap and the ammonia-forming pathway
units.guide: Urine anion gap = urinary Na⁺ + urinary K⁺ − urinary Cl⁻ = unmeasured anion − unmeasured cation, normally slightly negative. A positive UAG indicates RTA; a negative UAG indicates GI loss. Ammonia formation is predominantly in the proximal tubules from glutamine → glutamate → α-keto glutarate, releasing NH₃ at each step.
